summary: Janela Polar ("Polar Window") is a free web tool that shows, for any lunar landing site and date, when the Sun is up and when Earth is in view, using JPL Horizons ephemerides and real LOLA terrain. It compares Artemis III regions, recent landers, Apollo sites and your own coordinates side by side, finds the best landing dates, and links a launch delay directly to which site will be lit and in contact when you arrive.
details:
Project Description

The problem. At the lunar south pole the Sun never climbs more than 1–2° above the horizon, so a mountain 20 km away can decide whether a site has power for weeks or sits in darkness. Earth, needed for direct-to-Earth (DTE) radio, also hangs low and rocks up and down with libration. Existing tools (QuickMap, Moon Trek, Horizons) have the data, but comparing scenarios quickly is hard.

What we built.

  • Janela Polar — map of the south pole and of the whole Moon; for each site, Sun and Earth elevation and azimuth, countdowns to sunset and earthset, the next "ideal" window (Sun + DTE), the longest night, DSN antennas in view, and return windows. A horizon chart draws the real LOLA skyline with the Sun and Earth paths; a timeline shows Sun / DTE / Ideal / Return bands with a draggable cursor and animation; a heatmap finds the best landing date for a mission length; tables compare sites and pinned scenarios; anyone can add a coordinate.
  • Earth to Moon — Hohmann and 3-day transfers, return to entry interface with the Apollo daylight-recovery rule, launch sites. A launch delay moves the arrival date, and one click opens the surface view for that site and date.
  • NASA Data — every source explained, with per-site links to the official Horizons tables.
  • Three one-click guided scenarios for judges: a launch delay at Malapert, a 3 km ridge-vs-hollow contrast, and the far-side relay need of Chang'e 6.

What it shows. Two points 3.5 km apart in de Gerlache Rim 2 get 92 % vs 36 % sunlight over a month (longest night 2 days vs 19 days). A 5-day launch delay from 24 Nov 2026 cuts Malapert's Sun-and-Earth time from 97 % to 21 % — and switching to Mons Mouton does not fix it: it keeps the Sun but loses Earth even sooner, because libration drops Earth below the south-polar horizon in early December. Power and communication point to different answers.

How it works. Python/Flask backend calling the JPL Horizons API (airless, observer on the Moon), with a validated analytic fallback (Meeus) that also runs in the browser; horizon masks ray-cast from LOLA DEMs out to 150 km; Artemis III region centres from the official USGS grids; plain HTML/JS frontend that works offline and on GitHub Pages, refreshed daily with a Horizons bundle by GitHub Actions. English and Portuguese.

Validation. Against live JPL Horizons, 3 sites × 3 dates: worst difference 0.035° (tolerance 0.35°). 85 automated tests (Python and JavaScript) run on every push.

Impact. Mission planners can test dates and sites in seconds; teachers and the public can see why the south pole is different, in two languages, on a phone.
